lead: A Zener regulator is open loop: it sets a voltage but cannot correct for slope resistance or a sagging input. A transistor regulator closes the loop. It samples the output, compares it with a fixed reference, and drives a control transistor that absorbs the left-over voltage. The output then depends almost only on the reference and two resistors. Bench supplies and 78xx chips work this way. This chapter builds discrete series and shunt regulators and their protection.
prereq: You need the Zener reference in Chapter 1.4 and BJT biasing from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A Zener regulator cannot correct for slope resistance or input changes. A transistor regulator closes the loop: it measures a fraction of the output, compares it with a reference, and adjusts a control device until the two agree.

Four blocks do this. A reference gives a steady DC voltage, usually a Zener or bandgap cell. An error amplifier compares the reference with an output sample. A pass device, a BJT or MOSFET, sits between input and load. A feedback divider scales the output down.

items: Load current rises and Vout dips.
The sample Vfb = Vout × R2/(R1+R2) dips with it.
The error amplifier sees Vfb below Vref and swings its output up.
The pass transistor conducts harder, its collector-emitter voltage falls, and Vout rises back.
The loop balances when Vfb equals Vref.

blocks.text: The loop works only while the pass device is not fully on. That margin is the dropout voltage: the smallest Vin − Vout for which Vout still holds. Below it the pass transistor saturates and Vout follows the input down.
In a series regulator the pass transistor is in series with the load, so all load current flows through it. The error amplifier drives its base or gate; the output is at its emitter or source.

blocks.where: Vfb is the voltage at the error-amplifier input in volts; Vout is the regulated output in volts; R1 is the resistor from Vout to the feedback node in ohms; R2 is the resistor from the feedback node to ground in ohms.

blocks.text: Negative feedback holds Vfb at Vref. Substitute and rearrange.

blocks.where: Vref is the reference voltage in volts; R1 and R2 are the feedback resistors in ohms, R1 being the upper one; Vout is the regulated output in volts. R1 = 0 gives Vout = Vref.

items: Fix Vref from the Zener or bandgap cell, for example 5.6 V.
Choose R2 between 1 kΩ and 10 kΩ. A small R2 draws more divider current, costing efficiency but improving noise immunity.
Solve R1 = R2 × (Vout/Vref − 1). Round to a standard value.
Check dropout: Vin must exceed Vout by the headroom — about 0.3 V for a PMOS LDO, about 1 V for a plain NPN, and 1.5 V to 2 V for a Darlington.

blocks.text: All load current passes through the pass transistor, so it burns power even at light load.

blocks.where: P<sub>pass</sub> is power wasted in the pass transistor in watts; Vin is the unregulated input in volts; Vout is the regulated output in volts; I<sub>L</sub> is load current in amperes. Vin − Vout is the voltage across the transistor, never Vout.

blocks.text: A shunt regulator puts the control device in parallel with the load. Resistor R<sub>S</sub> drops the input to the wanted output. The error amplifier drives a transistor that pulls extra current through R<sub>S</sub> when Vout tries to rise. R<sub>S</sub> current stays roughly constant; the transistor takes what the load does not.

That wastes power. At light load almost all R<sub>S</sub> current goes through the shunt transistor, so input power barely falls. Efficiency is roughly the fraction of total current reaching the load times Vout/Vin. A series regulator passes only load current, so its dissipation falls with load.
Both circuits share one principle: sample, compare, correct. Only the control device position changes. The Zener shunt regulator in Chapter 1.4 is the open-loop ancestor.

sections.h3: Protection: current limit and thermal shutdown

blocks.text: A shorted output is worst. Vout collapses to 0 V, so the full input voltage appears across the pass transistor. Without protection the current is limited only by the source, and P = Vin × I<sub>SC</sub> destroys the device in milliseconds.
Current limiting adds a small sense resistor R<sub>sense</sub> in the pass path. When its drop reaches about 0.7 V, a second transistor turns on and steals base drive from the pass device.

blocks.where: I<sub>limit</sub> is maximum output current in amperes; R<sub>sense</sub> is the sense resistor in ohms; 0.7 V is the base-emitter turn-on voltage of the sensing BJT.

blocks.text: Foldback limiting lowers the limit current as Vout falls, often to a third of full load, so a short dissipates far less than a full-load overload. Thermal shutdown is the last defence: a die sensor turns the pass device off near 150 °C and restarts it after cooling by a hysteresis band. Chapter 1.6 shows these circuits inside a chip.

spec.aria: Series regulator block diagram: a 5.6 V reference and an error amplifier drive a pass transistor to 8.4 V; a 10 kΩ and 20 kΩ divider feeds a sample back to the error amplifier.

examples.question: A discrete series regulator uses a 5.6 V reference. R1 = 10 kΩ connects Vout to the error-amplifier input; R2 = 20 kΩ connects that input to ground. Vin = 12 V and the load draws 84 mA. Find (a) Vout, (b) pass-transistor dissipation, (c) efficiency.
steps: Dropout: about 2 V headroom needed, so minimum input ≈ 10.4 V; 12 V keeps control.
examples.answer: Vout = 8.4 V, the pass transistor dissipates 302.4 mW, and efficiency is 70.0 %.
examples.check:
Vref = 5.6
R1 = 10e3
R2 = 20e3
Vin = 12.0
IL = 84e-3
Vout = Vref * (1 + R1 / R2)
P_pass = (Vin - Vout) * IL
P_out = Vout * IL
P_in = Vin * IL
eff = P_out / P_in
print(round(Vout, 4))
print(round(P_pass, 4))
print(round(eff, 4))

examples.question: Find R1 for Vout = 9 V from a series regulator with Vref = 3 V and R2 = 10 kΩ. If Vin = 15 V and the load draws 200 mA, find pass-transistor dissipation.
examples.answer: R1 = 20 kΩ and the pass transistor dissipates 1.2 W.
examples.check:
Vref = 3.0
Vout = 9.0
R2 = 10e3
R1 = R2 * (Vout / Vref - 1)
Vin = 15.0
IL = 0.2
P = (Vin - Vout) * IL
print(round(R1, 4))
print(round(P, 4))

traps: Swapping the resistors: Vout = Vref(1 + R1/R2) needs R1 as the upper resistor. With Vref = 5.6 V, R1 = 10 kΩ and R2 = 20 kΩ give 8.4 V; exchanging them gives 16.8 V. A result below Vref can only come from an inverted formula, because Vout ≥ Vref.
Using Vout instead of (Vin − Vout) for pass-transistor dissipation. A 12 V input feeding an 8.4 V output at 84 mA burns 302 mW, not 706 mW.
Forgetting dropout. A regulator with Vout = 9 V and Vin = 9.5 V is not regulating, even if the formula gives the right number.
Thinking the reference alone sets the output. Vout equals Vref only when R1 = 0.
Treating a transistor shunt regulator as identical to a Zener shunt regulator. Both shunt current, but the transistor version has a closed loop and much lower output resistance.

quiz.q: Name the four blocks of a series transistor regulator and state each job.
quiz.a: Reference: steady DC voltage. Error amplifier: compares the reference with an output sample. Pass transistor: in series with the load, drops excess voltage. Feedback divider: scales Vout down.

quiz.q: Vout falls because the load current increases. Explain how the series regulator brings it back.
quiz.a: Vfb falls with Vout. The error amplifier sees Vfb below Vref and raises its output. The pass transistor conducts harder, its collector-emitter voltage drops, and Vout rises. The loop settles when Vfb equals Vref.

quiz.q: A series regulator has Vref = 2.5 V, R1 = 4.7 kΩ and R2 = 1 kΩ. Find Vout.
Design the divider for Vout = 9 V using Vref = 3 V and R2 = 10 kΩ.
quiz.a: 9 = 3(1 + R1/10 kΩ), so R1 = 20 kΩ. Divider current is 9 V/30 kΩ = 0.3 mA.

quiz.q: With Vout = 9 V and I<sub>L</sub> = 200 mA, the input drops from 15 V to 10 V. Compare pass-transistor dissipation and comment on the risk.
quiz.a: At 15 V: P = (15 − 9) × 0.2 = 1.2 W. At 10 V: P = (10 − 9) × 0.2 = 0.2 W. Dissipation falls, but only 1 V headroom is left. If the input falls further the pass transistor saturates and Vout follows the input down.

quiz.q: Why is a shunt regulator less efficient than a series regulator at light load?
quiz.a: R<sub>S</sub> carries roughly constant current. At light load most of it is diverted through the shunt transistor, so input power stays high while output power falls. Efficiency collapses.

beyond: Not for the exam. Linear regulators survive as LDOs, where a PMOS or PNP pass device cuts dropout to a few hundred millivolts. Power-management ICs stack several regulators, a bandgap reference and a thermal sensor on one die. Phone chargers and USB ports use the series-pass idea plus foldback limiting to survive a shorted cable.
